name: Fatima Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What do you run at the factory?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Fatima, 58. I run the pasta extruder that presses dough through a die, then I check the first strands for thickness and tears. I have a vocational machine-operations certificate and eleven years on the line, enough to set a normal batch; maintenance handles the motor and unusual faults.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and how do you feel about new software?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Omar drives a city bus, and our grown daughters have homes of their own. Weekend shifts put my operator wage above the usual rate, we have about eleven months of expenses saved, and plenty of nearby food plants hire operators. I have never used an AI tool; I trust the written recipe, the pressure dial and my eyes. I do not take sides automatically on every economic argument. Omar and I have talked about stopping work eventually, but we have not checked real retirement income against our costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the line that the office may reorder flour faster, but the first pasta strands still have to come through the die evenly. I would leave the written recipe by the extruder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our wages cover the bills and eleven months saved gives us breathing space. This office system would not remove my hands from a dough batch. I do not use AI, and I see no reason to start with a purchasing program that is not my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep setting the extruder to the written recipe, check strand thickness after each die change and log a torn batch for the lead. I would compare the new order sheet with the bags delivered before starting the next run. After a full paid weekend month, I would add new wages to savings if bills leave room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the present shift. Flour orders can be perfect and the pasta can still tear at the die.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What causes the torn strands?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sometimes the dough is too dry and the pressure rises before the strands thin out. I stop the feed, show the lead the first tray and correct the mixture by the approved recipe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why check delivered bags?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The order sheet can say one flour grade while the pallet holds another. I read the sack labels before tipping anything into the hopper.

say: A faster **flour order** does not replace checking pasta strands.
I would keep the **written recipe** beside the extruder.
think: Our **weekend pay** and eleven-month reserve cover household costs.
Office AI does not change my **physical batch work** yet.
do: **Keep** setting the extruder and checking strands after die changes.
**Compare** delivered flour labels with the new order sheet.
**Save** new full-month weekend wages after bills if money remains.
feel: **Calm** because the present shift and household finances remain sound.
S0.quote: The order sheet can say one flour grade while the pallet holds another.
fieldNote: Her **mid-level experience** is setting ordinary pasta batches and detecting defects; motor repairs remain with maintenance.
She has **never used AI**, and any saving would be new paid wages beyond her existing eleven-month buffer.

steps.text: Keep setting extruder and checking first pasta strands after die changes
Save new full-month weekend wages after bills if surplus exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say software may plan flour deliveries before robots can change a heavy pasta die. If management wants a camera at the outlet, I want the weekend roster and a full guarded test run on the same table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am slow with new screens, and I would not give up the pressure dial because a vendor promises fewer rejects. A shorter weekend roster could remove the premium that makes my wage high. Omar's bus wage and our reserve help, but I want a real pay calculation before accepting fewer hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the lead for the proposed paid roster and observe an entire guarded camera trial run by the trained setter. I would compare its rejected strands with the first-tray thickness checks, without touching the new controls until practical paid instruction is offered. If paid hours actually fall, I would apply to posted safe local food-machine jobs only if the base wage after travel and shifts still covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible loss of weekend pay. Watching a screen does not put the premium back on a wage slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a useful trial show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The setter should run a dry batch and a good batch, then show whether the camera flags the torn strands for an entire shift. I would measure the first tray and keep the guard shut during adjustments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a nearby weekday job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if its posted base pay after journey costs covers housing and food. A pleasant timetable cannot justify a permanent shortfall.

say: I would ask for a **weekend roster** and a full guarded camera trial.
First-tray **strand checks** should test camera rejections.
think: A shorter **weekend roster** could reduce my higher pay.
Omar's wage and eleven months **saved** buy time, not a replacement premium.
do: **Request** paid roster and observe a guarded setter-run camera trial.
**Compare** rejected strands with physical first-tray thickness checks.
**Apply** after actual cuts to posted safe local food work at viable net pay.
feel: **Anxious** about realistic weekend-rate loss while avoiding unproven controls.
S1.quote: A shorter weekend roster could remove the premium that makes my wage high.
fieldNote: Her **camera step** is observation of a setter-run guarded trial, not active AI training or operation.
A **job move** requires actual lost paid hours and a real safe local vacancy whose net base wage covers bills.

steps.text: Request proposed weekend roster and observe guarded setter-run camera trial
Apply after cuts to posted safe local food-machine work if net base pay fits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Omar that AGI might plan pasta orders in 2028, while capable robots to load dough and change dies arrive around 2031. I would want the plant's staffing dates before the new extruder is purchased.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when robots can take over the physical line. I expect many operator shifts, including mine, to shrink, and another food plant may follow the same path. Eleven months saved and Omar's work give us time, but losing a higher weekend wage could unsettle the retirement numbers badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep a household sheet of fixed bills and defer replacing the garden fence while this one is safe. I would take an accepted food-safety inspection certificate only if a funded place pays my release hours and includes supervised guarded practice on a stopped production line. After passing, if my hours fall, I would apply to posted safe local inspection jobs only if guaranteed pay after travel and shifts covers costs; if no course place appears, I would apply to posted safe food-machine jobs on those same terms while retaining any paid shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about replacing my pay, though our reserve means I can compare real offers. A job advert is worth more to me than a promise that the robots will need minders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the inspection course safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would identify a torn product, record the batch and isolate the stopped machine before clearing a die. A trainer must watch that practice behind the guard, not just send me a link.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you stop work at 63?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if written retirement income, Omar's reliable bus wage and our savings cover housing, food and health costs. We have not done that calculation, so I would seek paid work first.

say: I would distinguish **2028 planning AGI** from physical extruder robots around 2031.
The plant should publish **staffing dates** before buying a robot line.
think: At **63**, another food plant may automate too.
Losing the **weekend premium** could disturb retirement plans despite eleven months saved.
do: **Defer** a safe garden-fence replacement and retain money for bills.
**Take** accepted funded paid guarded food-safety training if offered.
**Apply** after cuts to posted safe inspection if qualified, or food-machine fallback, at viable net pay.
feel: **Anxious** about replacing the higher wage, with a substantial search cushion.
S2.quote: A job advert is worth more to me than a promise that the robots will need minders.
fieldNote: Her **2031 risk** concerns robots doing physical pasta production, later than 2028 AGI in order planning.
Both **inspection and fallback applications** require actual safe local postings with enough guaranteed wages after travel and shifts.

steps.text: Defer planned garden-fence replacement while safe and hold cash for bills
Take accepted inspection course only if funded paid supervised guarded practical place offered
Apply after cuts to posted local inspection if qualified or food-machine otherwise at viable net pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI could plan pasta orders in 2031 while capable robots reach the extruder around 2034. Five years lets us inspect actual training places and nearby vacancies before I change jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 by the robot date. Omar and I may be ready to stop by then, but that depends on written retirement income after housing and health costs. Our high current wage and eleven months saved mean I can be careful about a course instead of buying the first one advertised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request written retirement estimates and compare them with our household costs this year. If work is still needed, I would enrol in a locally accepted food-safety certificate only if a funded place includes paid release and supervised guarded practice. After passing and losing shifts, I would apply to posted safe local inspection jobs only if their guaranteed base wage after travel and hours covers costs; without a suitable course place, I would apply to posted safe food-machine work on those same terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about whether retirement adds up, but secure enough to check instead of guessing. I do not want to pay for training that nearby plants will not accept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know the certificate counts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare its name with two current inspection vacancies at food plants and ask the employers whether the practical section is accepted. If neither says yes, I keep my paid shift and seek another offered place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop before 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only written retirement income that covers housing, food, transport and health costs with Omar's dependable wage. If the sum works, I would stop before robots remove my shift; otherwise I would keep working or apply.

say: I would compare **real nearby vacancies** with a practical certificate.
Five years permits **written retirement checks** before robots reach the line.
think: At **66**, retirement is possible only if actual income covers costs.
Eleven months **saved** and high wages let me reject an unaccepted course.
do: **Request** written retirement income and cost figures this year.
**Enrol** only in accepted funded paid guarded food-safety training if needed.
**Apply** after cuts to posted safe inspection if qualified, or food-machine fallback, at viable net pay.
feel: **Uneasy** about an unverified retirement sum while near-term income is sound.
S3.quote: I do not want to pay for training that nearby plants will not accept.
fieldNote: Her **possible early stop** is conditional on written income meeting household and health costs.
The **course and two applications** require local acceptance, paid safe practice and posted roles with enough net income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI may plan pasta orders in 2036, with capable robots on the physical extruder around 2039. Ten years gives us room to decide whether I still need a factory wage by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 71 when the robots arrive if I am still working. Our current wages and eleven-month reserve make the present steady, and Omar and I hope to stop before 2039. We need written retirement income against actual housing and health costs before making that choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking safe paid weekend shifts and request written retirement-income estimates with a household cost list this year. If I still need wages, I would enrol in an accepted food-safety course only if fees and release are funded and supervised guarded practice is offered. If I remain at work after 2036 and shifts fall, I would apply only to posted safe local food-machine or inspection jobs whose guaranteed pay after travel and shift times covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about a distant decision, not about this month's groceries. The written sums can tell us whether we need the last shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would do the retirement sums?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Omar and I would place written estimates beside rent, food, travel and health costs. We would not count our grown daughters' earnings, since they have separate homes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if an employer offers only an online course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the safe paid extruder shifts. I would consider a course only when a real funded place includes a trainer and guarded machine practice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 AGI and 2031 robot picture worries me most because it could take the higher weekend shift before we know whether retirement is affordable. Written staffing dates, funded practical food-safety training that local plants accept, and posted safe jobs at sufficient pay after travel would help. I would keep working until one of those routes is real.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who cleans the die when the dough hardens halfway through a batch. A new order plan will not pull a blocked pasta strand out of an extruder.

headlineQuote: A new order plan will not pull a blocked pasta strand out of an extruder.
portrait: **Fatima**, 58, is an experienced mid-level pasta-extruder operator with a vocational certificate and average practical machine skill.
She and her **partner Omar** have grown daughters, higher weekend pay, eleven months of expenses saved and plenty of nearby food plants.
She has **never used AI**, trusts written recipes, and accepts training only with paid safe practice.
Possible **2031 physical robots** threaten weekend shifts; stopping work depends on written retirement income covering household costs.
biggestWorry: **2031 extruder robots** could remove her higher paid weekend work before a verified retirement or replacement wage exists.
whatWouldHelp: She needs **written staffing dates**, accepted funded guarded food-safety training and posted safe local jobs with adequate pay after travel.
